transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

Well… I suppose I’m here because I just don’t seem to sit still much anymore. For the past year or so I’m always puttering around—fixing things, arranging things, saying yes to another volunteer thing. Even at my age, I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Have you noticed any recent changes like unexplained weight loss, feeling unusually warm or sweaty, or your heart racing along with this restlessness?
No… I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed anything like that, at least not that I can say.
Along with this restlessness, do you also notice yourself feeling unusually worried or on edge much of the time?
Not really… I mean, I get bothered by things like anyone, but I wouldn’t say I’m unusually worried all the time.
Over this past year, have you noticed periods where you felt unusually upbeat, full of energy, or needed much less sleep than usual but still felt fine?
No, I don’t think so. My energy’s been… busy, I suppose, but I haven’t had times like that where I barely slept and felt wonderful or anything.
Have you started or changed any medications recently, especially anything like an antipsychotic, anti-nausea drug, or other new prescription?
No… not that I can think of. I don’t believe anything’s been changed recently.
Thinking back to when you were a child or teenager, do you recall having similar trouble sitting still, staying focused, or feeling restless back then?

Yes… I suppose so. In grade school I remember getting scolded for popping out of my seat and talking over other children. Teachers used to say I was “too lively,” that sort of thing… long before I was a teenager.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports chronic, pervasive hyperactivity/restlessness (difficulty sitting still, excessive activity, over-engagement in tasks) persisting for over a year, with clear childhood onset (grade school reports of being unable to stay seated, talking out of turn, being labeled 'too lively'). No evidence supports an alternative explanation: no manic/hypomanic episodes (denies elevated mood, decreased need for sleep), no generalized anxiety (denies pervasive worry), no medication-induced akathisia (no new drugs), and no hyperthyroid symptoms (denies weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance). This pattern of early-onset, persistent hyperactive-impulsive symptoms without mood or anxiety etiology is consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
